overview: Pictish communities and kingdoms occupied parts of early medieval Scotland. Evidence from Fortriu and Portmahomack reveals political centres, skilled workshops and religious learning, while the later emergence of Alba represents a complex transformation with uncertain frontiers.

items.text: References to Picts appear from the late third century. The archaeological transition into early medieval societies remains debated; this is not a secure kingdom foundation date.
By the seventh century Fortriu had emerged as a powerful Pictish kingdom, now located around the Moray Firth. Its extent and internal divisions remain uncertain.

Power centres shifted south in the later ninth century. By the tenth, parts of the Highlands came under Alba's control or influence, often intermittently; this does not establish a single conquest date for all Picts.

Around 700 Portmahomack developed stone carving, metal and glass working, and hide processing interpreted as parchment production. Together with its cemetery and infrastructure, these remains support identification as a monastery.
After destruction around 800, workshops resumed activity. A Viking raid is a possible explanation for the destruction, not an identified event that ended every Pictish polity.

Bede reports that King Naiton requested guidance on calculating Easter and asked Ceolfrid for builders of a stone church. The account connects royal patronage with calendar learning and technical exchange.
